chunks: "An AC coupling capacitor goes in series with a signal path. It passes the changing part of the signal and blocks the DC part.

That lets me connect two circuits that sit at different DC levels without one disturbing the other's bias, like a microphone into an amplifier, or a sensor that swings around zero into a single-supply input that biases at half the rail.
Electrically it forms a high-pass filter with the resistance after it, so it isn't an on-off switch.
The corner is f equals one over two pi R C, where R is the input resistance the capacitor drives, usually the bias network in parallel.
Below that frequency the signal is attenuated, and above it it passes.

So I choose C based on the lowest frequency I want to keep: for 20 hertz audio into a 5 kilohm bias network, I want the corner well below 20 hertz, say 3 to 5 hertz, so around 8 to 10 microfarads, and a 2.
2 microfarad part would give a corner at 14 hertz and attenuate 20 hertz by almost 2 decibels.

Costs: a bigger capacitor means a longer startup, because it charges through R with tau equals R C, so tens of milliseconds, and polarized electrolytics need the right DC polarity, leak a bit, and can add distortion.
And I always need to provide a DC bias path after the cap, so the node doesn't float."
